en: The *Pudāwang jīng* (Sutra of King Universal Attainment), translated by an unknown person, now appended to the Catalogue of the Western Jin:
Thus have I heard: At one time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the kingdom of Wénwù at the Jìshì tree grove.
The Lonely One was dwelling together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a king of the country of Puyen, named Puda, who governed various states and received tributes from the four quarters.

The King himself reverently upheld the Buddha and the Honored Dharma, never once acting with partiality or injustice. He always maintained a compassionate heart, feeling pity for the ignorant common people who did not know the Three Honored Ones. Whenever it was time for the fast and purification, he would ascend a high place to observe and burn incense; then, returning, he would prostrate himself with his head to the ground, performing the ritual of bowing in salutation.
The ministers and subjects within the kingdom marveled at the King’s behavior and deliberated among themselves, saying:

"The King occupies the most honored position among the myriad people; he is revered and submissive to by those far and near, and his words are followed by all. What request or desire could he have that would lead him to humiliate his majestic dignity by prostrating himself with his head to the ground?"
The ministers deliberated among themselves repeatedly, desiring to offer counsel but not daring to do so.
The King commanded his subordinates to prepare for the journey; the King then set out from the palace with several thousand officials and commoners.

Before they had gone far, they suddenly saw a practitioner of the Way. The king immediately descended from his carriage and set aside his parasol; he halted his retinue and prostrated himself with his head to the ground to pay homage to the practitioner. He then followed him back, prepared a meal for him, and consequently could not proceed on his journey.
Thereupon, the ministers remonstrated, saying:
"O Great King, Most Exalted One!
Why should you on this road bow your head to the ground before such a mendicant practitioner?"
"In all the world, nothing is more noble than the head; furthermore, as the sovereign of a kingdom, it is not the same as that of others.
The king then commanded his ministers to seek the heads of dead men, as well as the heads of oxen, horses, pigs, and sheep.
The subordinate officials immediately went everywhere to search for them; after many days, they finally obtained them and returned to report to the king, saying:
"We have received your previous command to seek the heads of dead men and the heads of the six domestic animals; we have now obtained them all."
The king said, "Sell it in the marketplace.
The ministers immediately dispatched people to sell it; the heads of oxen, horses, pigs, and sheep were all sold, yet there remained one human head that had not been sold.
The king said,
"Whether sold by the lowly or the noble, ensure that it is sold;
if it does not sell, then give it as alms to others."
As the days passed in this manner, the goods could not be sold, nor was there anyone to take them as alms; the heads all became swollen and so foul-smelling that they were unbearable to approach.
The King then grew greatly incensed and said to his ministers:
"You officials previously advised me, saying:..."
"The human head is the most precious; it must not be defiled or insulted by placing it upon the ground to prostrate before a practitioner.
Now, when one tries to sell the heads of domestic animals, they are all purchased; why then do people refuse to take a human head even when begging for it?
The king immediately commanded his ministers to prepare the carriage, intending to go outside the city to a vast marsh to inquire about something.
The assembled ministers and the people were all struck with awe and trembling, not yet knowing the king’s purpose.
The king immediately led his retinue out beyond the city walls and addressed his ministers, saying:
"Do you recognize that young boy who used to carry my late father's parasol?"
The minister replied,
"I truly am aware of it. The King said:
"Where is this child now?
He replied, "He has been gone for a long time; seventeen years have already passed."
The king asked,
"As for this child's character, is he good or evil? They replied:

"Your subjects have often observed him serving the former king; he maintained his fasts and purifications with reverent gravity, preserved his integrity and sincerity, and spoke nothing that was not in accordance with the Dharma.
The King said to his ministers, "If you were now to see the clothes this boy wore when he was alive, would you recognize them?"
The ministers replied,
"Although it has been a long time, we still recognize it.
The king looked toward his attendants and ordered them to return immediately to the inner treasury to fetch the clothes of the son who had previously perished.
In a brief moment, the robe arrived, and the king asked,
"Is this indeed it? The ministers replied:
"It is indeed his robe.
The King asked,
"If you were now to see the boy's body, would you recognize it?"
The ministers all remained silent; after a long while, they replied, "We ourselves feared our own ignorance and were unable to distinguish what we suddenly beheld.

Just as the King was about to explain the original transformation, the practitioner he had previously seen arrived. The King was greatly delighted and rose, prostrating himself with his head to the ground to pay homage to the practitioner; among the ministers, there was none who did not rejoice.
The practitioner took his seat, and the king, with palms joined, said:

"Previously, when I was traveling on the road, I encountered you, O practitioner; I immediately turned back to return home, yet I was mocked and found strange by my ministers and subjects, who admonished me, saying:
'The human head and face are the most honorable and noble.'"
Furthermore, as a ruler of the state and sovereign of the myriad people, you are one toward whom the four quarters turn in devotion.
Why do you beg for what you desire and prostrate yourself before this mendicant?
I then issued an order that the heads of the six domestic animals and human heads be sold together in the marketplace.

While the heads of the six domestic animals all found buyers, there was no one who would purchase the human heads; even beggars would not take them, for they were what these people held most precious.
I have now come forth in solemn array, desiring also to demonstrate the origins and the end of this matter.

It is my great fortune that you, O Master of the Way, would deign to lower your dignity; I pray that you will guide the ignorant subjects and citizens of this kingdom, enabling them to know the True Dharma and leading them across the bridge of the present.
The practitioner then explained to his subordinates the former transformation of the king:

"If you wish to know who this king was, he was originally a young boy who held a parasol for the former king. He constantly followed the former king in observing the fast and precepts for one day, practicing the True Dharma, maintaining purity and guarding his mind, and refraining from all evils."
"After passing away in that previous life, his soul returned to birth as the son of a king.
That he has now attained such high honor and nobility is entirely due to the merit of his past practice of fasting and precepts.
Thus spoke all the officials, high and low, in unison.
"We are fortunate to have encountered and beheld a man of the Way; we pray that you will take pity on our ignorance and folly, and deign to accept us as your disciples.
The man of the Way told the ministers and citizens:
"I have a Great Master from whom I should receive instruction; you must go to him for questions."
The ministers replied,
"We wish to hear what the Great Master intends to practice.
We would all exhaust our lifespans just to have the opportunity to personally attend upon him and receive his teachings."

The practitioner replied: "My teacher is titled 'Buddha. His body is capable of flying, and his crown is encircled by a halo of light. He can divide his body and disperse his form, manifesting ten thousand transformations. He possesses thirty-two extraordinary marks and eighty minor characteristics. He presides over the heavens and earth and the twelve thousand realms; he walks alone through the three worlds with no one equal to him. His disciples are pure and are called śramaṇas; the teachings he imparts for their deliverance are never in vain."
The subordinate official then addressed the practitioner,
saying, "May we have the opportunity to see the Buddha?
The practitioner replied:
"Excellent! We shall go and inform the Venerable One.
The ministers then asked the practitioner:
"Where is the Buddha currently located, and how far is it from here?
The practitioner replied,
"It is more than six thousand *li* away."
In the brief span of a moment, the practitioner flew to the kingdom of Śrāvastī and reported in detail to the Buddha:
"The people of that country are truly pitiable; they now all sincerely desire to see the Buddha."
"Please, out of your great compassion, reveal and show us the true path.
The Buddha remained silent for a moment, then called to Ānanda:
"Command the bhikṣus that tomorrow we shall go to the kingdom of Vairambhya."
Ānanda, having proclaimed the Buddha’s teaching, returned and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are the ritual procedures for tomorrow?
The Buddha said:
"As he approaches, he shall manifest his majestic spiritual power. At that time, the Buddha was accompanied by the bhikṣus;

before they had yet traveled several tens of *li*, the king and his ministers all followed the mendicant. Carrying flowers and incense, they went out of the city to welcome the Buddha. Beholding the Buddha’s majestic aura, joy and trepidation welled up within them simultaneously. Prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, they bowed their heads in homage and escorted the Buddha up to the hall to take his seat.

The king knelt before the Buddha with palms joined and addressed him, saying, "I am deeply honored that the World-Honored One and the assembly of monks have condescended to travel so far to this place.
The king and his ministers were filled with fear and did not know what to do; the Buddha, perceiving their thoughts, spoke immediately to Ānanda:
He said to the king, "Do not worry that the preparations will not be complete; for wherever the Buddha goes, how could there be any lack?
The king served with all his heart, personally pouring out the drinks and food; when the meal was finished, he offered water for washing.
When the incantation and prayer were concluded, the Buddha smiled, and five-colored light issued from his mouth. Ānanda adjusted his robes, prostrated before the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"The Buddha does not smile without cause; surely there is something he intends to say."
The Buddha said,
"Do you wish to know the origins and history of King Puhada and the mendicant? Ānanda replied:
"I wish to hear the details of this matter.
The Buddha said:

"In the past, during the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Buddha, there was a king who was the son of a prominent family. His father made offerings to the Triple Gem and commanded his son to pass on the incense."

At that time, there was an attendant who, in his heart, looked down upon him and did not give him any incense. Because sin and merit respond like echoes, he incurred this calamity; yet, although he was briefly employed as a servant, he never forgot to uphold the Dharma, and now he has become a king presiding over the people. You should know that this is the result of what one has established for oneself; therefore, be careful not to act with partiality.
The practitioner was originally a servant; at that time he did not receive any incense. Although he did not receive any incense, his mind harbored no resentment, and he immediately made a vow:
"If I attain the Way, I shall deliver this person."
"The convergence of merit, vows, and their fruits has now brought me here to deliver you, O King, as well as your people.

When the king heard the Buddha’s account of the beginning and end of these events, his mind was liberated and he immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna. Upon hearing this sutra, the people of the kingdom all received the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths, making them their constant practice.
At that time, the fourfold assembly of disciples, having heard the sutra, rejoiced; they came forward, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
*The Sutra of King Puda*.
